notes: Printed page number = PDF page − 2 throughout.

Capacity figures use Cleanview project-level data accessed on September 12, 2026; the paper stresses the pipeline is 'not a completion forecast: projects may be delayed, reduced in scale, or never completed' and the 188.3/114.9/213.5 GW split is 'a scenario rather than a forecast' (PDF p.6).

Narrative rounding: the introduction (PDF p.3) rounds the scenario to '188 GW of new capacity', '$9.0 trillion in investment', 'averaging 3.22 percent of GDP per year', and 'a further 115 GW completed after 2032'; the precise values 188.3 / $8.973 trillion / 3.22% / 114.9 appear in Section II (PDF pp.6–7).
Equation (1) (PDF p.26): I_s = 0.72195·c_s·K_s + 0.17561·c_{s+1}·K_{s+1} + 0.05122·c_{s+2}·K_{s+2} + 0.05122·c_{s+3}·K_{s+3}; the paper states the shares verbally on PDF p.25.
The 1.10 million racks / 79.3 million GPUs are stated in Appendix D (PDF p.31) as a conversion 'Using the GB300 NVL72 configuration in Appendix A'.
1,515 TWh (2025) is the annual electricity of the entire U.S. residential sector, used as the full-utilization analog for capacity completed by 2032 (PDF p.4, Section I).

provenance.quote_en: we estimate approximately 63 GW of operating U.S. data center capacity and a development pipeline of approximately 494 GW, comprising 47 GW under construction and 447 GW planned.

provenance.quote_en: Our central scenario implies that 188.3 GW of additional U.S. capacity becomes operational during 2025–32, including 22.5 GW associated with projects already operational in 2025 or 2026.
A further 114.9 GW is completed after 2032, while 213.5 GW is never completed.
Our implied cancellation rate is 32.6% of projects, exactly in line with Brandsaas et al. (2025)’s 33% number based on historical cancellation rates from Dodge Construction Network data
capacity-weighted cancellation rate is 43.2%, incorporating both cancellation and downsizing.
